g12-geography-ug3-t1.overview: Sustainable development asks how humanity can develop economically and socially today without using up the environment that tomorrow's people will need. This lesson traces the history of the idea, its three interlocking pillars, the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, and how Ethiopia has integrated them into its national development frameworks.
objectives: Explain the meaning of sustainable development and the definition given in Our Common Future
Trace the sequence of UN conferences that developed the concept from Stockholm 1972 to Johannesburg 2002
Describe the three essential dimensions of sustainable development and how they relate as nested rings
Identify the Sustainable Development Goals adopted by the United Nations in 2015
Evaluate the integration of the SDGs in Ethiopian national development frameworks such as GTP II
g12-geography-ug3-t1.simple: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The term was first used in 1987 by the World Commission on Environment and Development, known as the Brundtland Commission after its chair, Gro Harlem Brundtland. The idea rests on three pillars: economic development, social development and environmental sustainability, often drawn as nested rings in which the economy depends on society and the environment. The world built the idea through UN conferences in Stockholm (1972), Nairobi (1987), Rio de Janeiro (1992) and Johannesburg (2002). In 2015 the United Nations adopted 17 Sustainable Development Goals with 169 targets to be achieved by 2030, and Ethiopia has integrated them into GTP II and its ten year development plan.
g12-geography-ug3-t1.detailed:
Historical overview. The concept of sustainable development emerged as one of the development paradigms that generated a rich literature, policies and programs by a wide range of international and national governmental bodies and NGOs. The first United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) was held in Stockholm in 1972; it introduced the notion of ecodevelopment and led to the establishment of UNEP, the United Nations Environment Programme, with a mission of providing leadership and encouraging partnership in caring for the environment by inspiring, informing and enabling nations and peoples to improve their quality of life without compromising that of future generations.

The term is born in 1987. The second UNCED, held in Nairobi, Kenya in 1987, introduced the idea of sustainable development. The term was first used in 1987 by the World Commission on Environment and Development, also known as the Brundtland Commission after its chair, Gro Harlem Brundtland. In its report Our Common Future, the Commission defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. This definition is rooted in systems thinking, stressing interdependency of the pillars.

The Earth Summit and Agenda 21. The third conference was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, known as the Earth Summit. It further developed Agenda 21, which highlighted the connection between poverty and underdevelopment on the one hand, and the connection between environmental protection and natural resource management on the other. Agenda 21 states in its Principle 1 that human beings, the centre of concern for sustainable development, are entitled to a healthy and productive life in harmony with nature.

The Johannesburg Summit. The fourth conference, the World Summit on Sustainable Development, was held in Johannesburg, South Africa in 2002. This summit placed much more emphasis on the social and economic aspects of sustainable development. Another formulation states that a development path is sustainable if total welfare does not decline along the path; welfare depends on consumption, environmental quality, social equity and other quality-of-life factors.

The three dimensions. An economic system must produce goods and services on a continuing basis, keep government and external debt at manageable levels, and avoid extreme sectoral imbalances that damage agriculture or industry. An environmental system must maintain a stable resource base, avoid overexploitation of non-renewable resources, and preserve biodiversity, atmospheric stability and ecosystem services. A social system must achieve fairness in distribution and opportunity among all persons, with adequate provision of health, education and gender equity. Sustainable development aims to bring the three together as interconnected nested rings: the economy is inside society, and society inside the environment, because the economy depends on both.

The SDGs and Ethiopia. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), also called the Global Goals, were adopted by the United Nations in 2015 as a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet and ensure that by 2030 all people enjoy peace and prosperity. The 2030 Agenda comprises 17 goals and 169 targets, from No Poverty and Zero Hunger through Clean Water and Sanitation, Gender Equality and Climate Action to Partnerships for the Goals. In Ethiopia the FDRE appreciated the contribution of the SDGs to its aspiration to eradicate poverty, and integrated them into GTP II, implementing them nationwide from the 2015/16 fiscal year, notably SDG 4 (equitable quality education), SDG 6 (water and sanitation) and SDG 7 (affordable reliable energy). The Climate-Change-Resilient Green-Economy strategy (CRGE), the Paris Agreement and the national disaster prevention and management policy have also been implemented. After governance reform in 2018 the GTP evolved into a homegrown economic reform, and the new ten-year development plan of 2021-2030 contemplates the SDG pillars, keeping agriculture as the mainstay of development, transforming manufacturing, building a climate resilient green economy and eliminating rent-seeking behaviour.

Shortcomings of the notion. Critics point to the incorrectness of the term sustainable development and its internal logical contradiction; the narrowness that confines global problems to the environmental context; the opinion that implementation can benefit only part of humanity rather than all people; the controversial character of several methods used; and the diversity in understanding the goals that arises from different worldviews. Yet critics and followers are united in believing that the transition to sustainable development requires a dramatic transformation of the current civilization, whose core is the environmentalisation of all major human activities.

workedExamples.problem: A geography teacher asks you to place the four major UN conferences that built the concept of sustainable development in chronological order, giving each its contribution.
workedExamples.given: Stockholm 1972; Nairobi 1987; Rio de Janeiro 1992; Johannesburg 2002.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: sequence events by the years cited in the source and match each with its landmark output.
workedExamples.calculation: 1972 Stockholm introduced ecodevelopment and UNEP; 1987 Nairobi and the Brundtland Commission introduced sustainable development; 1992 Rio produced Agenda 21; 2002 Johannesburg emphasized social and economic aspects.
workedExamples.answer: Stockholm (1972), Nairobi (1987), Rio de Janeiro - Earth Summit (1992), Johannesburg (2002).

workedExamples.problem: Classify the following as belonging to the economic, social or environmental dimension: (a) keeping external debt at a manageable level, (b) gender equity in schooling, (c) preservation of biodiversity.
workedExamples.given: Three statements and the three dimensions of sustainable development.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: match each policy concern to its pillar.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) concerns goods, services and debt; (b) concerns fairness and social services; (c) concerns ecosystems and resource base.
workedExamples.calculation: Debt and sectoral balance belong to the economic system; equitable provision of education and gender equity belongs to the social system; biodiversity belongs to the environmental system.

workedExamples.problem: The 2030 SDG Agenda comprises 17 goals and 169 targets. On average, how many targets does each goal carry?
workedExamples.formula: Average targets per goal = total targets / total goals.
workedExamples.calculation: 169 / 17 = 9.94, rounded to about 10 targets per goal.

workedExamples.problem: A district triples its harvest by clearing all forest and draining wetlands, but this exhausts the resources its children will inherit. Using the textbook definition, judge whether the district is on a sustainable development path.
workedExamples.given: Welfare rises today but the natural resource base declines sharply.
workedExamples.formula: Test: a development path is sustainable if total welfare does not decline along the path.
workedExamples.substitution: Present gains are outweighed by a destroyed environmental pillar.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the needs of future generations cannot be met when forest and wetlands are gone, the path fails the intergenerational equity test.
workedExamples.answer: Not sustainable; it violates future generations' ability to meet their own needs.

commonMistakes: Claiming the term sustainable development was first used at the 1972 Stockholm Conference instead of by the Brundtland Commission in 1987.
Saying the Earth Summit was held in Johannesburg; the Earth Summit was Rio de Janeiro 1992, while Johannesburg 2002 hosted the World Summit on Sustainable Development.
Treating sustainable development as only an environmental matter and forgetting the economic and social pillars.
Viewing the three pillars as separate silos instead of nested, interdependent rings where the economy depends on society and the environment.
Confusing the number of SDGs (17) with the number of targets (169).
Assuming sustainable development means stopping all economic growth rather than balancing growth, society and environment.
applications: Linking a local school, water point or clinic project to specific goals such as SDG 4, SDG 6 or SDG 3 on Good Health and Well-Being.
Assessing Ethiopia's Climate-Change-Resilient Green-Economy strategy as a national expression of sustainable development.
Debating whether the ten-year development plan of 2021-2030 balances the economic, social and environmental pillars.
Weighing a proposal to expand farmland by asking whether future generations' access to forest and wetlands is preserved.
Applying the SDG principle of prioritizing progress for those furthest behind when designing a community intervention.
g12-geography-ug3-t1.summary: Sustainable development, first named in 1987 by the Brundtland Commission in Our Common Future, means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It unites economic, social and environmental dimensions as nested rings, and it matured through the 1972 Stockholm, 1987 Nairobi, 1992 Rio and 2002 Johannesburg conferences. The United Nations adopted 17 SDGs with 169 targets in 2015, which Ethiopia has integrated into GTP II, the CRGE strategy and its 2021-2030 development plan.

g12-geography-ug3-t2.overview: Conflicts over land, water and minerals are among the most common causes of tension and violence worldwide. This lesson explains the types of natural resources, the categories and drivers of resource conflict, transboundary disputes including the Nile Basin, and the sustainable livelihoods approach to preventing conflict.
objectives: Classify natural resources into renewable and non-renewable categories using regeneration capacity
Identify the categories of resource conflicts and their main drivers
Analyze the three main drivers of conflict over renewable resources, including the three types of scarcity
Examine transboundary resource dynamics and the record of water cooperation and conflict
Apply the sustainable livelihoods framework to conflict prevention in an Ethiopian context
g12-geography-ug3-t2.simple: Natural resources come in two broad groups based on regeneration capacity. Renewable resources, or flow resources, replenish themselves through reproduction or recycling and include biotic resources like plants and animals plus abiotic ones like solar energy, land, soil, water and air. Non-renewable, or fixed and fund resources, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and metals, form slowly and once used up are gone forever. Conflicts typically involve extractive resources, land or water, and turn on ownership, access, decision making and distribution of revenues. Three main drivers of conflict are competition over increasingly scarce renewables, poor governance, and transboundary pressures such as the Nile. The sustainable livelihoods framework and community-oriented interventions help prevent conflict because no quick technical fix exists alone.
g12-geography-ug3-t2.detailed:
Meanings and types of resources. A resource is any element or substance useful for the satisfaction of human requirements. On the basis of regeneration capacity, natural resources fall into two broad categories. Renewable resources are recurrent, replenishing themselves in the foreseeable future; they are also called flow resources and regenerate through reproduction or recycling. They comprise all biotic resources, such as animals and vegetation, and most abiotic resources, such as solar energy, land and soil, water and air. Non-renewable resources do not regenerate by natural processes; called fixed or fund resources, they were formed slowly and their supply is limited by nature, so once they are used up they are gone forever. This category includes most minerals: coal, petroleum, natural gas, and ferrous and non-ferrous metals.

Categories and drivers of resource conflict. Resource conflicts are categorized by the primary resource involved and the main conflict driver. Typical categories are extractive resources such as hydrocarbons, minerals, gemstones and timber, land, and water. Conflicts over renewables are essentially political issues: who should have access to and control over the resources, whose views should count in prioritizing problems, and what rates of use are desirable? In the majority of cases one or more of four drivers are at play: conflict over resource ownership, over resource access, over decision making about management, and over distribution of revenues, benefits and burdens. These disputes involve a wide range of actors, from nation-states and local governments to ethnic groups, communities, civil society and private companies, and often show power imbalances, for example international corporations versus local communities.

Unique characteristics. The scarcity or abundance of a resource influences the conflict dynamics and mediation opportunities. Resource disputes often involve uneven geographic patterns of distribution, which become salient when they occur along ethnic, religious or linguistic lines. Tensions over scarce resources often run in seasonal cycles and can escalate into violence after sudden shocks or stresses. Natural resources can trigger, intensify or prolong conflicts, and in many situations they reinforce the power of elite actors within the broader political economy; rights are often governed by a combination of customary and statutory institutions, or hybrid political orders.

The three main drivers. Working alone or together, three drivers have contributed to violent conflict when acting alongside socio-economic, political and security stresses: (1) competition over increasingly scarce renewable resources, (2) poor governance of renewable natural resources and the environment, and (3) transboundary natural resource dynamics and pressures. Resource scarcity describes a situation where the supply of water, forests, rangelands and croplands is insufficient to meet local demand. Responses to rising competition include migration, technological innovation, cooperation and violent conflict. Scarcity itself has three causes: demand-induced scarcity when population growth, higher consumption or new technologies cut per capita availability; supply-induced scarcity when environmental degradation, natural variation or breakdown in delivery infrastructure reduces total supply; and structural scarcity when different groups face unequal access, for example where women face restrictions in purchasing land, drilling water wells or harvesting resources, or where poverty blocks buying the equipment needed to exploit a resource.

Poor governance. Four types of grievance lead to poor resource and environmental management: unclear, overlapping or poor enforcement of resource rights and laws, where land is regulated under a combination of statutory, customary, informal and religious tenure and the state lacks capacity to enforce rules in rural areas; discriminatory policies, rights and laws that marginalize specific groups; unequal distribution of the benefits and burdens of development projects, where extractive industries pollute or exhaust resources without compensation, or damage resources with cultural or spiritual meaning; and lack of public participation and transparency in decision-making, which causes communities to oppose decisions made with private actors behind closed doors.

Transboundary dynamics. Managing renewables often extends beyond national borders, especially for water, wildlife, fisheries and air quality. Under the UN Charter, states have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources but the responsibility not to cause damage to the environment of other states. Four transboundary pressures cause conflict: one country consuming shared resources at higher rates and violating agreed allocations; the quality or quantity of resources being damaged by infrastructure, industry or land-use change, such as pollution crossing borders or deforestation and soil erosion heightening hazard vulnerability in a neighbour; migrating pastoralists and wildlife crossing borders along traditional routes based on water and grazing availability; and illicit extraction and trade of resources by criminal groups, which deprives local communities of benefits. The record is instructive: there are 263 rivers that cross or demarcate international boundaries; cooperation over shared waters has outnumbered conflict by more than two-to-one over the past fifty years; since 1948 only 37 incidents of acute conflict over water were recorded (30 of them involving Israel, the last in 1970), while some 295 international water agreements were negotiated in the same period. Yet 158 of the 263 international basins lack any cooperative management framework.

The Nile Basin and conflict prevention. Transboundary water management is a key diplomatic issue among the eleven countries sharing the Nile Basin. The Nile Basin Initiative (NBI) was formally established in 1999 to coordinate basin management and promote peace and security, and it was the first initiative to include all basin states. Upstream countries request an agreement on equitable share, sustainable food production through irrigation, a mechanism facilitating hydroelectric power construction, and collaboration on soil and water conservation. In 2010, five upstream states signed the Nile River Basin Cooperative Framework for an equitable share, though Egypt and Sudan strongly opposed it. International law guides coexistence: ILC Article 5 requires equitable and reasonable utilization of international watercourses, Article 7 the obligation not to cause significant harm, Article 8 the obligation to cooperate, Article 9 the exchange of data and information, and Article 20 the protection and preservation of ecosystems. There is no quick fix: the technical side of natural resource management cannot be separated from institutional and governance aspects, so conflict prevention requires technical, political and institutional responses together. The sustainable livelihoods framework, with its five capitals (Human, Natural, Financial, Social, Physical) and vulnerability context, is used by UN agencies and donors to design prevention through five approaches: livelihood diversification (multi-sectorial, multi-locational, multi-occupational), improving efficiency and added value along the value chain, livelihood adaptation programmes for climate change and disasters, protecting livelihoods from eroding, and emergency livelihood support such as food distribution, water, sanitation, shelter and health care.

workedExamples.answer: About 105 basins, roughly 40 percent of the total.

workedExamples.answer: 7 incidents, the last of which occurred in 1970.

commonMistakes: Treating every natural resource as renewable and forgetting that minerals and hydrocarbons are fixed or fund resources.
Confusing demand-induced scarcity (rising demand per capita) with supply-induced scarcity (falling supply from degradation or infrastructure breakdown).
Thinking resource conflicts are purely technical rather than political questions of access, control and priorities.
Assuming shared rivers cause mainly conflict, when cooperative interactions over the past fifty years outnumbered conflictive ones by more than two to one.
Mixing up the four conflict drivers (ownership, access, decision making, revenue distribution) with the three main drivers (scarcity, poor governance, transboundary pressures).
Believing resource scarcity has only one cause instead of three that can work separately or in combination.
applications: Analyzing a local grazing or irrigation dispute by asking which of the four conflict drivers is at play.
Applying ILC Articles 5, 7, 8 and 9 to argue Ethiopia's case for equitable and reasonable use of the Nile.
Using structural scarcity to explain why marginalized groups in a community depend unequally on the same forest or rangeland.
Designing livelihood diversification (agricultural plus non-farm, on-farm plus off-farm work) to reduce vulnerability to resource scarcity in a farming area.
Anticipating transboundary tensions when upstream water use or upstream deforestation changes the flow and quality of a shared river.
Evaluating whether a development project distributes its benefits and burdens fairly, since unequal sharing is a key grievance that fuels conflict.
g12-geography-ug3-t2.summary: Resources are renewable (flow) or non-renewable (fixed and fund), and conflicts over extractive resources, land and water are driven by disputes over ownership, access, decision making and revenues. Three drivers fuel conflict: competition over scarce renewables caused by demand-, supply- and structural-induced scarcity, poor governance with four classic grievances, and transboundary pressures that are best met by cooperation, of which the Nile Basin and its 1999 Initiative are leading examples. The sustainable livelihoods framework offers prevention through diversification, efficiency, adaptation, protection and emergency support.

g12-geography-ug3-t3.overview: How power and decisions over land, water and minerals are shared determines whether exploitation brings development or conflict. This lesson defines natural resource governance, examines the rights of indigenous communities, and sets out the four governance challenges and five principles of good governance of natural resources.
objectives: Define natural resource governance and explain why it is increasingly contentious
Describe the protection of indigenous communities' tenure rights under UNDRIP and the CBD
State the three pillars of public participation advanced by the Aarhus Convention
Identify the four governance challenges that often lie at the root of resource conflicts
Explain the five principles for improving the governance of renewable natural resources
g12-geography-ug3-t3.simple: Natural resource governance is the set of norms, institutions and processes that determine how power and responsibilities over natural resources are exercised, how decisions are taken, and how citizens, including women, men, indigenous peoples and local communities, participate in and benefit from management. It is contentious because of over-exploitation, environmental degradation and destroyed livelihoods. Indigenous communities are hit hardest by monoculture farming, industrial fishing, logging, mining and dam construction, so governance must respect self-determination and tenure rights, as demanded by Article 10 of UNDRIP and the Convention on Biological Diversity. Four governance challenges lie at the root of most resource conflicts, and good governance responds with five principles: clarifying rights, equitable access, impact assessments, genuine public participation, and readiness for unexpected impacts.
g12-geography-ug3-t3.detailed:
What natural resource governance is. Natural resource governance refers to the norms, institutions and processes that determine how power and responsibilities over natural resources are exercised, how decisions are taken, and how citizens, women, men, indigenous peoples and local communities participate in and benefit from the management of natural resources. It becomes increasingly contentious in view of the over-exploitation of resources, the environmental degradation resulting from excessive farming and mining, and the destruction of livelihoods where such exploitation takes place. Improving governance, including securing rights and sharing power and responsibilities, can benefit both people and biodiversity through improved ecosystem health and human wellbeing.

Why governance matters for conservation. Land use debates in conservation, wildlife protection and sustainable development revolve strongly around governance because the prioritization, allocation and management of resources directly affect the environment and its inhabitants. Implicit in these debates is the call for exploitation to be carried out in a manner that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Robust laws, institutions, policies and processes can reduce populations' vulnerability to resource scarcity and resolve disputes over access, ownership, control and management; yet because conflicts are highly context dependent, no two governance solutions are ever the same.

Indigenous communities and their rights. Indigenous communities are particularly affected by exploitation such as monoculture farming, industrial fishing, logging, mining and dam construction, so a central feature of governance pertains to indigenous self-determination and tenure rights. Sadly, many national legal frameworks still do not sufficiently recognize customary lands and environmental stewardship. Article 10 of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) states that indigenous peoples should not be forcibly removed from their lands, and where relocation occurs it must follow free, prior and informed consent together with fair and just compensation. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) recognizes that communities are inextricably linked to their territories and that preserving traditional knowledge is crucial to conservation and biological diversity.

The Aarhus Convention pillars. Where consultation is denied, a sound governance framework should provide administrative or legal avenues of redress. Article 1 of the Aarhus Convention (the UNECE Convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters) advances three pillars: the right of access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice, as means to empower communities to protect their own environments. In sum, governance should embody principles that promote environmental sustainability and recognize tenure rights and cultural integrity, fostering bottom-up, consensus-oriented decision making among multiple stakeholders premised on trust, shared commitment and common understanding.

Four governance challenges. Four challenges often lie at the root of conflicts over natural resources: (I) unclear, overlapping or poor enforcement of resource rights and laws; (II) discriminatory policies, rights and laws that marginalize specific groups; (III) unequal distribution of benefits and burdens from development projects; and (IV) lack of public participation and transparency in decision-making.

Five principles to improve governance. First, there must be legal and institutional changes to clarify resource rights, responsibilities, laws and institutional mandates, clearly recognizing and respecting the rights of poor and marginalized people who depend directly on natural resources. Second, at the national level equitable resource access should be a priority of public policy, measured against socio-economic inequality, poverty and livelihood vulnerability, and then improved through measures linked to sustainable livelihoods and poverty reduction. Third, the legal framework should require environmental and social impact assessments for all major development projects, including infrastructure, industrial sites and major extractive industries, conducted transparently with key stakeholders and made publicly available. Fourth, governance should increase opportunities and requirements for public participation in decision-making and resource management, for which community-based and collaborative management approaches are often used. Fifth, even where rights are clarified, assessments are conducted and participation is enhanced, unexpected impacts on renewable resources can emerge as a normal part of the development process, so governance must remain capable of responding to them.

From governance to peace. Good governance is one of the fundamental preconditions of sustainable development. Factionalism and the competition and clash of priorities are problems in any governance framework; improving the basic governance of renewables reduces vulnerability, prevents conflict and creates space for dispute resolution; since governance challenges are context dependent, each country and community must adapt these principles to its own laws, landscapes and cultures.

keyTerms.def: The norms, institutions and processes that determine how power and responsibilities over natural resources are exercised and how citizens participate in and benefit from their management.
The recognized claims of people and communities, including customary owners, to hold, use and benefit from land and resources.
The right of indigenous peoples to determine their own development priorities and govern their lands and resources.
The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 2007, protecting indigenous land rights and consent.
The consent requirement of UNDRIP Article 10 before indigenous peoples may be relocated, together with fair and just compensation.
The UNECE Convention guaranteeing access to information, public participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters.
A required, transparent, stakeholder-inclusive assessment of major development projects before and during implementation.
A collaborative approach that involves local communities directly in natural resource decisions and management.

workedExamples.problem: A mining company plans a large project in a rural district. It publishes the design, invites affected communities to comment, and promises compensation for damages. Which governance challenge is it trying to avoid, and using which intervention?
workedExamples.given: The company works through transparency, participation and compensation.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: match the company's measures to the four governance challenges and five principles.
workedExamples.substitution: Transparency and comment address lack of public participation and unequal distribution of burdens.
workedExamples.calculation: Publishing information plus consultation plus compensation satisfies public participation, transparency and impact assessment requirements.
workedExamples.answer: It avoids challenges III and IV (unequal benefits and burdens; no participation), using the third and fourth principles: impact assessment with stakeholders and genuine public participation.

workedExamples.problem: A government official withholds the findings of a project study from the community and pushes approval through a small committee. Which Aarhus pillars are violated?
workedExamples.given: Information is withheld and the community cannot contribute or appeal.
workedExamples.formula: Test each Aarhus pillar: access to information, public participation, access to justice.
workedExamples.substitution: The withheld study blocks pillar one; the closed committee blocks pillar two; the absence of redress blocks pillar three.
workedExamples.calculation: All three pillars fail because the community cannot see the data, cannot influence the decision and cannot seek redress.
workedExamples.answer: All three pillars: access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice.

workedExamples.problem: A hydropower project wants to relocate an indigenous village whose elders were never consulted, although planners claim the project benefits the whole nation. Judge the case using UNDRIP Article 10.
workedExamples.given: Relocation is planned without free, prior and informed consent or agreed compensation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: UNDRIP Article 10 forbids forced removal; relocation requires free, prior and informed consent and fair compensation.
workedExamples.substitution: No consultation occurred and no compensation was agreed.
workedExamples.calculation: The relocation fails both consent and compensation requirements, so it breaches Article 10.
workedExamples.answer: The project must stop until full, free, prior and informed consent and fair and just compensation are secured.

workedExamples.problem: Two districts both suffer conflicts over a shared rangeland. In district A the resource rights are written clearly; in district B laws are overlapping and unenforced. Predict which governance challenge dominates in each and the likely first intervention.
workedExamples.given: District A: rights clear, conflict persists; district B: unclear and overlapping laws.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: align the observed problem with the four governance challenges.
workedExamples.substitution: District B shows unclear, overlapping and poorly enforced rights; district A must face discrimination or unequal benefit sharing.
workedExamples.calculation: District B needs legal and institutional changes to clarify rights; district A should assess inequitable access and participation.
workedExamples.answer: District B: challenge I, so clarify rights first (principle one). District A: challenges II to IV, so work on equitable access, impact assessment and participation.

commonMistakes: Thinking governance means only government action, when it also covers indigenous peoples, local communities, civil society and the private sector.
Believing environmental and social impact assessments are optional if a project is profitable.
Confusing token consultation with genuine public participation as required by the Aarhus Convention pillars.
Forgetting that indigenous relocation requires free, prior and informed consent plus fair and just compensation, not merely payment after eviction.
Memorizing the four governance challenges but failing to connect each one to the matching governance principle.
Assuming perfect institutions can be prescribed, when no two governance solutions are ever the same because conflicts are context dependent.
applications: Reviving zak or shimglina-type local redress mechanisms where the right to consultation is denied, as avenues of justice.
Demanding that a kebele assembly see the impact assessment of a proposed factory or dam before it is approved.
Using the three Aarhus pillars to organize a community campaign around a polluted river or fence line.
Checking a national park plan to confirm that indigenous and local communities keep tenure rights and cultural integrity.
Pushing for environmental and social impact assessments to be conducted transparently and published publicly.
Assessing new distribution of benefits from a mining project so poor and marginalized groups and biodiversity both gain.
g12-geography-ug3-t3.summary: Natural resource governance is the set of norms, institutions and processes deciding how power over resources is exercised and how all citizens participate in and benefit from management. UNDRIP Article 10, the CBD, the three Aarhus pillars and bottom-up consensus-oriented decision making protect indigenous peoples and communities. Good governance confronts four root challenges - unclear rights, discrimination, unequal benefits, and exclusion - through five principles: clarifying rights, equitable access, impact assessment, public participation, and capacity to handle unexpected impacts.

g12-geography-ug3-t4.overview: Long before, and alongside, formal courts, Ethiopian communities have settled disputes over land, pasture and water through elders and customary law. This lesson surveys indigenous mechanisms such as Shimagle, Gadaa, Mada'a, T'eer and Gumma, compares them with the formal legal system, and reviews the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
objectives: Explain why indigenous mechanisms are widely used to prevent and resolve resource conflicts
Describe the role of the Fetha Negast and the Shimagle in settling disputes at local level
Identify the indigenous institutions of Ethiopian pastoralists, including T'eer, Gadaa, Mada'a, Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba
Compare the outcomes of formal legal processes with indigenous conflict resolution
Evaluate the relevance of UNDRIP articles to indigenous conflict resolution
g12-geography-ug3-t4.simple: Societies worldwide have long used indigenous mechanisms to prevent and resolve conflicts, often based on community customs and familial relationships. In Ethiopia most rural communities take complaints to elders and customary processes rather than the police. Because the country is multi-ethnic, each group has its own system: the Fetha Negast encouraged amicable local settlement through elders called Shimagle; the Oromo use the Gadaa system and Gumma; the Somali use T'eer law and the guurti council of elders; the Afar rely on the Mada'a. These systems are governed by unwritten law transmitted orally from generation to generation and yield win-win outcomes, while formal courts are often inaccessible, slow and produce winner-takes-all results. UNDRIP, adopted in 2007, further protects indigenous rights to land, consultation and fair conflict resolution.
g12-geography-ug3-t4.detailed:
Why indigenous mechanisms matter. Societies worldwide have long used indigenous mechanisms to prevent and resolve conflicts, often based on community customs, familial relationships or institutional practices, running alongside formal state-sanctioned processes. In a society where the majority of the populace is poor, with widespread illiteracy culminating in lack of access to justice and the high cost and scarcity of lawyers, traditional conflict resolution stands out as the best method. In Ethiopia, many rural and village communities do not refer complaints to the police or prosecuting authorities but deal with them through indigenous tribal processes.

Rooted in culture, not uniform. Indigenous mechanisms are deeply rooted in the culture and traditions of different ethnic groups; they gain legitimacy from community values rather than the state. Because Ethiopia is multi-ethnic, the mechanisms differ from ethnic group to ethnic group and do not have uniform application across the country. In ancient times, especially under the Fetha Negast (the law of the kings), conflicts between individuals or communities were encouraged to be settled amicably at local level; elders, called Shimagle, or people appointed on an ad-hoc basis, played an important role, and the practice is still widespread, as Figure 3.5 shows in Sidama, Ethiopia and northern Kenya, where elders seek solutions to conflict over land, pasture and water. Even after a case has passed through criminal court procedures and penalties, people use indigenous mechanisms for reconciliation and to reduce acts of revenge.

Pastoral institutions. The Gadaa among the Oromo and the Shimagle among the Amhara and other groups are well-known. Pastoral communities also have well-developed systems involving elders and clan leaders under traditional law: the T'eer of the Somali, the Gadaa system of the Oromo and the Mada'a of the Afar are governed by unwritten law transmitted from generation to generation orally. Somali, Borana and Afar pastoralist institutions are led respectively by Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba, and each community keeps two types of law: one concerning intra-ethnic group disputes and one concerning inter-ethnic group disputes.

How the systems work. In Afar, conflicts between clans are managed by the Mada'a based on customary law and elders who are selected from different clans, not representing members in disputes. The council's decisions are effective because of the tradition of forgiveness, respect for elders, and the transfer of resources as compensation; the Mada'a once managed conflicts effectively between the Afar and some of their neighbours. Among the Oromo, Gumma is a conflict resolution technique related to killing, particularly unintentional killing of a person from another clan or within the same clan; it helps prevent the grievances and revenge that often follow such a killing. For the Somalis, the guurti, the council of elders, acts as judges and jury under their customary law, and its decisions are largely adhered to and respected; elders prevent conflict by monitoring and punishing individuals who plan to trigger it and by pressing clans to honor inter-clan agreements.

Indigenous versus formal systems. Formal legal systems have weak points: courts are inaccessible in pastoral areas and justice is a lengthy process. Formal resolution rests on a fixed code of law and is unlikely to consider long-standing social and economic relations among community members; moreover, government legal setups often produce a zero-sum, winner-takes-all outcome because they serve justice through imposed agreements and never target reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. In some instances the formal system even refers cases back to elders' councils, showing that indigenous mechanisms bridge the gap in the formal system. Indigenous resolution, on the contrary, leads to win-win situations because it weighs the interests of every party: disputants acknowledge they have something to gain and something to lose, especially in inter-clan conflicts, where government institutions serve as auxiliaries to elders' mediation.

The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2007, the Declaration makes direct reference to indigenous peoples' rights to land and self-determination, the two issues at the heart of most conflicts affecting indigenous peoples. Article 7 recognizes their collective right to live in freedom, peace and security as distinct peoples free from any act of violence including forcibly removing children of the group to another group; Article 30 asks states to undertake effective consultations through their representative institutions before using their lands or territories for military activities; Article 32 states that indigenous peoples have the right to determine and develop priorities and strategies for the development or use of their lands and resources; and Article 40 guarantees access to prompt, just and fair procedures for resolving conflicts with states, and to effective remedies for infringements of their individual and collective rights.

keyTerms.def: Conflict settlement based on community customs, familial relationships and customary institutions rather than state courts.
The law of the kings, under which conflicts were encouraged to be settled amicably at local level.
The elders, or ad-hoc appointed elders, who settle disputes in Amhara and other communities.
The Oromo indigenous system of governance and conflict resolution.
The customary law institution managed by elders selected from different clans, used by the Afar to manage inter-clan conflicts.
The conflict resolution law of the Somali, transmitted orally from generation to generation.
The Oromo conflict resolution technique related to unintentional killing, which prevents grievances and revenge.
The council of elders of the Somali, acting as judges and jury under customary law.

workedExamples.problem: Match each Ethiopian group with its customary conflict resolution institution: (a) Oromo, (b) Somali, (c) Afar, (d) Amhara.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: link each mechanism to the ethnic group named in the textbook.
workedExamples.substitution: Gumma relates to unintentional killing; T'eer is Somali law; Mada'a manages Afar clan conflicts; Shimagle is the elders' system used by the Amhara.
workedExamples.calculation: Each mechanism matches exactly one group's customary institution.
workedExamples.answer: (a) Oromo - Gadaa and Gumma, (b) Somali - T'eer with the guurti, (c) Afar - Mada'a, (d) Amhara - Shimagle.

workedExamples.problem: In two communities, one dispute ends with a court judgment that arrests one young man and awards land to the winner; a second dispute among the same clan and neighbouring clan ends when elders secure an apology and compensation in livestock, and families resume sharing a water point. Identify the type of outcome produced by each path.
workedExamples.given: Path one is a formal court; path two is elders' mediation.
workedExamples.formula: Test: does the outcome produce a winner-takes-all result or a win-win reconciliation?
workedExamples.substitution: Court: winner takes all through imposed agreement. Elders: both parties give and gain something.
workedExamples.calculation: Formal systems produce zero-sum outcomes and rarely target reconciliation; indigenous mechanisms consider the interests of every party.
workedExamples.answer: Path one: zero-sum, winner-takes-all. Path two: win-win reconciliation that preserves coexistence.

workedExamples.problem: A quarrel between herdsmen from the same clan ends with the unintentional killing of a young man. Elders fear another round of deaths through revenge. Using the Oromo mechanism named in the textbook, propose the process.
workedExamples.given: The killing was unintentional and within or between clans.
workedExamples.formula: Match the case to Gumma, the Oromo technique for unintentional killing.
workedExamples.substitution: Gumma deals with unintentional killing and prevents the grievances and revenge that often follow such killing.
workedExamples.calculation: Applying Gumma turns the case from revenge into a settlement mediated before grievances harden.
workedExamples.answer: Convene a Gumma settlement by elders, preventing grievances and revenge through apology and compensation.

workedExamples.problem: Matching exercise: link (a) Ogaz, (b) Abbaa Gadaa, (c) Kedo Abba to the correct group among Somali, Borana and Afar.
workedExamples.given: Three leaders and three pastoralist groups.
workedExamples.formula: Skill: associate each title with its community of use.
workedExamples.substitution: The textbook lists Somali, Borana and Afar pastoralists led by Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba respectively.
workedExamples.calculation: Respectively means the pairing runs in the same order as the list.
workedExamples.answer: Ogaz - Somali; Abbaa Gadaa - Borana; Kedo Abba - Afar.

commonMistakes: Confusing the institutions: T'eer is the Somali law itself, while Ogaz leads the Somali institution; Mada'a is the Afar customary law, not a Somali one.
Assuming Ethiopia has one uniform indigenous system for all ethnic groups, when mechanisms differ from group to group and are not uniformly applied.
Believing indigenous law is written down and codified like statutory law; it is unwritten and transmitted orally.
Thinking formal courts always deliver reconciliation, when they often end in zero-sum, winner-takes-all outcomes through imposed agreements.
Forgetting that elders' decisions work because of the tradition of forgiveness, respect for elders and the transfer of resources as compensation, not because of state enforcement.
Assuming Gumma refers to land disputes, when it specifically addresses unintentional killing and prevents revenge.
applications: Inviting respected elders to mediate a neighbourhood or family dispute before it escalates to violence.
Using the Shimagle approach to reconcile parties after a court case reduces cases of revenge in the community.
Strengthening the role of Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba institutions in grazing and water disputes among pastoralists.
Recognizing that formal courts can refer some cases to elders' councils, bridging the gap in access to justice in remote areas.
Respecting indigenous land and self-determination rights as guaranteed by UNDRIP Articles 7, 30, 32 and 40.
Considering long-standing social and economic relations between groups, which formal courts overlook, when designing peace interventions.
g12-geography-ug3-t4.summary: Ethiopia's indigenous mechanisms, from the Fetha Negast's Shimagle to the Oromo Gadaa and Gumma, the Somali T'eer with its guurti elders, the Afar Mada'a with its Ogaz, Abbaa Gadaa and Kedo Abba leadership, settle land, pasture and water disputes on the basis of unwritten, orally transmitted law. They produce win-win reconciliation, while formal courts are slow, inaccessible and yield winner-takes-all results. The 2007 UNDRIP safeguards indigenous rights to freedom, consultation, self-determination and fair conflict resolution.
